layout.title: How to Calculate Your Calorie Needs? Complete Guide
layout.intro: Your calorie needs depend on your basal metabolic rate (BMR), activity level and goal — weight loss, maintenance or muscle building. This guide explains step by step how to calculate your individual calorie needs using scientific methods.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your calorie needs directly with our TDEE calculator

faq.question: How do you calculate your calorie needs?
faq.answer: You calculate calorie needs in three steps: 1) Calculate your BMR (basal metabolic rate) using the Mifflin-St Jeor formula based on weight, height, age and gender. 2) Multiply BMR by an activity factor (PAL 1.2–1.9) to get TDEE — your actual calorie needs per day. 3) Adjust for your goal: eat below TDEE for weight loss, above for bulking, or match it to maintain weight.

faq.question: How many calories does a woman need per day?
faq.answer: The average woman needs 1,800–2,200 kcal/day depending on age, height, weight and activity level. This is not an exact number — individual calorie needs can differ by 400–600 kcal between two women of the same body weight if they have different activity levels. Use the TDEE calculator for your individual figure.

faq.question: How many calories does a man need per day?
faq.answer: The average man needs 2,200–2,800 kcal/day. Just like for women, it varies significantly with activity level, muscle mass and age. A sedentary man at 70 kg might have a TDEE of 1,900 kcal, while an actively training man at 90 kg might have a TDEE of 3,200 kcal.

faq.question: What happens if you eat too little?
faq.answer: If you eat too little for a long time (significantly below TDEE) you risk: muscle mass loss as the body breaks down muscle for energy, adaptive thermogenesis where BMR drops, nutritional deficiency if the calorie amount doesn't cover essential vitamins and minerals, and hormonal disruptions (lower leptin, testosterone, thyroid hormones). A moderate calorie deficit of 300–500 kcal/day is sustainable; extreme restriction is not.

sources.text: Mifflin MD, St Jeor ST, Hill LA, Scott BJ, Daugherty SA, Koh YO. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals. Am J Clin Nutr. 1990;51(2):241–247.
Pontzer H, et al. Daily energy expenditure through the human life course. Science. 2021;373(6556):808–812.
Hall KD, et al. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826–837.

schema.headline: How to Calculate Your Calorie Needs? Complete Guide
schema.description: Learn how to calculate your individual calorie needs — from BMR and TDEE to calorie deficit and bulking.

s1.p1: BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate, basal metabolism) is the calories your body burns at complete rest — only to keep the heart, brain and organs running. It is the foundation for all calorie calculations.
s1.p2: The most widely used and validated formula for most adults is Mifflin-St Jeor:
items: Men: BMR = (9.99 × weight) + (6.25 × height) − (4.92 × age) + 5
Women: BMR = (9.99 × weight) + (6.25 × height) − (4.92 × age) − 161
s1.note: Weight in kg, height in cm, age in years.

s2.h2: Step 2: Calculate your TDEE with activity factor
s2.p1: TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is your total calorie need — BMR multiplied by your PAL factor (Physical Activity Level).
tableRows: Office or home work, little daily movement, no training
Light exercise 1–3 days/week, e.g. walks, yoga or gym in spare time
Regular exercise 3–5 days/week with moderate intensity, e.g. running or strength training
Hard training almost every day (6–7 days/week) or physically active work
Heavy physical work combined with daily intense training, e.g. elite athletes or construction workers who also train
s2.example: Example: A person, 30 years old, 80 kg, 180 cm, trains 3–5 times/week (moderately active).

s3.p1: Eat 300–500 kcal below your TDEE. That gives about 0.3–0.5 kg of weight loss per week — slow enough to preserve muscle mass. Combine with adequate protein (1.6–2.2 g/kg) for best results.
s3.p2: Eat 200–400 kcal above your TDEE. That creates a small surplus for muscle growth with minimal fat gain. More than 500 kcal/day in surplus often leads to unnecessary fat storage.
s3.p3: Match your TDEE. Great during rest periods, rehabilitation or to stabilise weight after a longer phase.

s4.h2: Why doesn't the calculator always match?
s4.p1: TDEE calculators provide an estimate with a margin of error of typically ±10–15%. Factors that affect the real value:
items: Muscle mass (more muscle = higher BMR)
Thyroid hormones and other hormonal balance
Sleep quality
Thermic effect of food (proteins require more energy to digest)
Adaptive thermogenesis (body lowers metabolism during prolonged calorie deficit)
s4.tip: Use the calculator as a starting point. Monitor your weight for 2–3 weeks and adjust the calorie goal if you don't see the expected result.

seo.title: What is TDEE? Total Daily Energy Expenditure Explained | CalculEat
seo.description: TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is the calories your body burns per day. Learn how TDEE is calculated and how to use it for weight loss or muscle building.

layout.title: What is TDEE? Total Daily Energy Expenditure Explained
layout.intro: TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is the total amount of calories your body burns over the course of a day, including all movement and activity. It is your maintenance need — and the starting point for counting calories whether your goal is weight loss, muscle building or maintaining weight.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your TDEE directly with our free calculator

faq.question: Is TDEE the same as calorie needs?
faq.answer: Yes, in practice the terms are used synonymously. TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is the scientific term for your total daily energy needs — the number of calories you burn during a day including all activity.

faq.question: How accurate is a TDEE calculator?
faq.answer: A TDEE calculator provides an estimate based on statistical formulas — Mifflin-St Jeor for BMR multiplied by a PAL factor (1.2–1.9) for activity level. Margin of error is typically ±10–15%. Individual factors such as muscle mass, hormonal balance and metabolism affect the true value. Use the result as a starting point and adjust based on how your weight actually changes.

faq.question: What is the difference between BMR and TDEE?
faq.answer: BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) is the calories your body burns at complete rest — only to keep organs running. TDEE also includes all physical activity, NEAT (unplanned movement) and TEF (thermic effect of food). TDEE is always higher than BMR and is the relevant number for calorie planning.

faq.question: How does TDEE change with age?
faq.answer: TDEE typically decreases with age for two reasons: BMR drops slightly per decade (primarily due to decreased muscle mass), and most people's activity level decreases. Strength training and adequate protein intake can significantly slow both processes.

faq.question: Why can two people of the same weight have such different calorie needs?
faq.answer: Muscle mass is the most important factor — muscles burn more energy at rest than fat. Activity level is the second most important. Two people of the same weight can have 500–800 kcal difference in TDEE if one trains actively and the other is sedentary.

FAO/WHO/UNU. Human energy requirements. Report of a Joint Expert Consultation. Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1. Rome, 2004.
von Loeffelholz C, Birkenfeld AL. Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis in Human Energy Homeostasis. In: Feingold KR, et al., editors. Endotext. South Dartmouth (MA): MDText.com, Inc.; 2022.
Levine JA. Non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT). Best Pract Res Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2002;16(4):679–702.
Westerterp KR. Diet induced thermogenesis. Nutr Metab (Lond). 2004;1(1):5.
Pontzer H, et al. Daily energy expenditure through the human life course. Science. 2021;373(6556):808–812.
Ainsworth BE, et al. 2011 Compendium of Physical Activities. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2011;43(8):1575–1581.
Speakman JR, Selman C. Physical activity and resting metabolic rate. Proc Nutr Soc. 2003;62(3):621–634.

schema.headline: What is TDEE? Total Daily Energy Expenditure Explained
schema.description: TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is the calories your body burns per day. Learn how TDEE is calculated and how to use it.

s1.p1: TDEE is calculated as the sum of four physiological components. Each component represents a unique part of the body's energy expenditure without overlap:

s1h3a.h3: BMR — Basal Metabolic Rate (approx. 60–75% of TDEE)
s1h3a.p1: BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) is the energy the body requires to maintain basic physiological functions at complete rest — breathing, blood circulation, temperature regulation and cellular processes. The most important determinant of BMR is fat-free mass, which is estimated to explain around 80% of the variation.
s1h3a.p2: In people with low physical activity, BMR typically constitutes about 60% of total energy expenditure, and even more in individuals with very low movement activity such as sedated and mechanically ventilated patients in intensive care units.
s1h3a.p3: BMR is measured under strictly controlled laboratory conditions: after sleep, in a fasting state and in a thermoneutral environment. In practical contexts, RMR (Resting Metabolic Rate) is more commonly used, measured at any time during the day, which can differ from BMR by up to 10%. Most online calculators — including CalculEat — technically calculate RMR, but use the term BMR in everyday use.
s1h3a.p4: The gold standard for measurement is indirect calorimetry via Weir's equation (1949). When unavailable, predictive equations such as Mifflin-St Jeor, Harris-Benedict or Cunningham are used, which have a margin of error of ±10–15% at the individual level.

s1h3b.p1: NEAT encompasses all energy expenditure from bodily movements that are not planned exercise: walking, standing, household chores, fidgeting and postural adjustments. It is the most variable component — and the most underestimated.
s1h3b.p2: In normally active individuals, NEAT constitutes approximately 15–30% of TDEE, but the variation is extreme. In very inactive individuals, NEAT can be as low as 6–10%, while in active individuals it can exceed 50% of total energy expenditure. In a controlled overfeeding study, the change in NEAT ranged from −98 to +692 kcal/day between individuals with similar body composition (Levine et al., 1999). Total differences in NEAT between individuals can amount to over 1,000 kcal/day.
s1h3b.p3: It explains why two people of identical weight and training routine can have such different calorie needs — the difference lies in spontaneous movement outside the gym, not in the training sessions.

s1h3c.p1: EAT represents energy expenditure from planned physical exercise. It typically constitutes a surprisingly small proportion of TDEE — under 5% in sedentary individuals. At high training volumes, EAT can increase to 15–30% or more in elite athletes (Westerterp, 2013).

s1h3d.p1: TEF is the energy required for digestion, absorption and metabolism of nutrients. Under energy balance, TEF averages about 10% of energy intake, with a typical range of 8–15% depending on meal composition.
items: Protein: approx. 20–30% — amino acid metabolism and urea formation are energy-intensive
Carbohydrates: approx. 5–10%
Fat: approx. 0–3% — low thermogenic effect
s1h3d.p3: The practical consequence: a protein-rich diet genuinely produces slightly higher energy expenditure at the same calorie intake compared to a fat-dominated diet (Westerterp, 2004; Halton & Hu, 2004).

s2.p1: The simplest method is BMR × PAL factor:
items: Calculate BMR with Mifflin-St Jeor (recommended for healthy adults)
Multiply by a PAL factor (Physical Activity Level) that reflects your activity level

s3.h2: How do you use TDEE in practice?
items: Weight loss: Eat 300–500 kcal below TDEE → approx. 0.3–0.5 kg/week
Muscle building: Eat 200–400 kcal above TDEE → lean bulk with minimal fat gain
Maintenance: Eat at TDEE → stable weight
s3.p2: The calculator provides an estimate with a margin of error of ±10–15%. Monitor your weight for 2–3 weeks and adjust if the result doesn't match expectations.

s4.h2: Why does TDEE drop during a diet?
s4.p1: Adaptive thermogenesis — the body lowers its metabolism in response to prolonged calorie deficit. It happens at several levels: NEAT decreases (the body instinctively moves less), BMR drops slightly and digestive efficiency increases. NEAT is the component that reacts fastest and most — and it is also why weight loss slows down despite unchanged intake.
s4.p2: Solution: take regular "diet breaks" (shorter periods at maintenance intake) to counteract the adaptation, and prioritise strength training to preserve muscle mass and keep BMR up.

seo.title: How Large a Calorie Deficit for Weight Loss? | CalculEat
seo.description: How large a calorie deficit is appropriate? Scientific guidelines for pace, protein and sustainable weight loss without losing muscle.

layout.title: How Large a Calorie Deficit for Weight Loss?
layout.intro: A calorie deficit of 300–500 kcal per day below your TDEE is the scientifically recommended pace for sustainable weight loss without losing muscle. It gives about 0.3–0.5 kg of weight loss per week — fast enough to see results, slow enough for the body to adapt healthily.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your exact calorie intake with the calorie deficit calculator

faq.question: What is a safe calorie deficit per day?
faq.answer: 300–500 kcal/day is the scientifically recommended range for sustainable weight loss for most healthy adults. It gives 0.3–0.5 kg of weight loss per week with minimal muscle loss. A deficit of more than 1,000 kcal/day significantly increases the risk of muscle mass loss and adaptive thermogenesis.

faq.question: How fast can you lose weight with a calorie deficit?
faq.answer: With a deficit of 500 kcal/day you lose about 0.5 kg of fat per week (500 × 7 = 3,500 kcal ≈ 0.5 kg fat mass). In reality, weight loss varies due to water retention, glycogen changes and adaptations. Expect 0.3–0.7 kg/week as a realistic range.

faq.question: Should you eat back calories after exercise?
faq.answer: It depends on your calculation method. If you've calculated TDEE with NEAT and exercise activity already included — no. If you've calculated a lower baseline TDEE and add exercise separately — yes. The most common mistake is double-counting activity and then eating back calories you haven't actually burned.

faq.question: What happens if you eat too little for a long time?
faq.answer: With prolonged aggressive deficit (>1,000 kcal/day for many weeks), the body lowers its metabolism via adaptive thermogenesis. NEAT decreases, BMR drops slightly, and energy expenditure during exercise can decrease. A diet break of 1–2 weeks at maintenance intake every 8–12 weeks counteracts this.

sources.text: Hall KD, et al. Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight. Lancet. 2011;378(9793):826–837.
Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ. Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11:20.
Trexler ET, Smith-Ryan AE, Norton LE. Metabolic adaptation to weight loss: implications for the athlete. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11(1):7.

schema.headline: How Large a Calorie Deficit for Weight Loss?
schema.description: Scientific guidelines for calorie deficit, pace and sustainable weight loss without losing muscle.

s1.p1: Weight loss is not only about losing weight on the scale — it's about preserving muscle mass and losing fat. If you lose weight too quickly, the proportion of muscle mass you lose increases, which impairs your metabolism long-term and makes it harder to maintain weight afterwards.
s1.p2: Don't lose more than 0.5–1% of body weight per week.

deficitLevels.title: Mild: 200–300 kcal/day
deficitLevels.desc: Suitable for beginners, close to competition or if you have little fat to lose. Very low risk of muscle mass loss.

deficitLevels.title: Moderate: 300–500 kcal/day
deficitLevels.desc: The scientific standard. Balance between pace and muscle mass preservation. Works for most people.

deficitLevels.title: Aggressive: 500–1000 kcal/day
deficitLevels.desc: Acceptable at high body fat percentage. Requires high protein intake (2.0–2.2 g/kg) and strength training to protect muscle mass.

s3.h2: The role of protein during a calorie deficit
s3.p1: The most important thing you can do to preserve muscle mass during a diet is adequate protein intake. Research supports 1.6–2.2 g protein per kg body weight per day.
s3.p2: Protein also has high satiety effect and high TEF (approx. 25–30% of protein calories are used to digest the protein) — making it extra valuable during a calorie deficit.

s4.h2: Adaptive thermogenesis — why does weight plateau?
s4.p1: With prolonged calorie deficit, the body lowers its metabolism as a defense against starvation. You instinctively move less (NEAT decreases) and BMR drops slightly. This is normal and not a sign that something is wrong.
s4.p2: Take a "diet break" for 1–2 weeks at maintenance intake (your TDEE) every 8–12 weeks. This restores hormonal balance, reduces adaptive thermogenesis and makes the next diet phase more effective.

items: Calculate your TDEE with a calculator
Subtract 400 kcal for a good starting pace
Eat 1.8–2.2 g protein per kg body weight
Strength train 2–4 times/week to protect muscle mass
Adjust the calorie goal every 2–3 weeks based on actual weight development
Plan in a diet break every 8–12 weeks

seo.title: Bulk and Cut — Calories for Muscle Building and Fat Loss | CalculEat
seo.description: How bulk and cut work, how many calories to eat in each phase and how to optimize your training cycle for muscle building and fat loss.

layout.title: Bulk and Cut — Calories for Muscle Building and Fat Loss
layout.intro: Bulk and cut are the two phases in a classic training cycle. During a bulk you eat in a calorie surplus to maximize muscle building. During a cut you eat in a calorie deficit to lose fat and preserve the muscle mass you've built. The key is knowing exactly how large a surplus and deficit to aim for.

faq.question: How long should you bulk before cutting?
faq.answer: A typical bulk phase lasts 3–6 months. Stop and enter a cut when body fat has risen to 18–20% (men) or 28–30% (women), or when you've reached your desired body weight. Alternatively: run 3-month cycles (bulk 3 months, cut 3 months) and keep body fat stable over time.

faq.question: Can you build muscle and burn fat at the same time (body recomposition)?
faq.answer: Yes — but primarily for beginners, those returning to training after a break, or those with high body fat percentage. For well-trained individuals the effect is small and slow. Body recomposition requires a neutral or minimal calorie surplus (±100 kcal), high protein (1.8–2.2 g/kg) and progressive strength training.

faq.question: How much muscle can you expect to build during a bulk?
faq.answer: Natural lifters can expect: beginners 1–1.5 kg of muscle mass per month, intermediate 0.5–1 kg/month, advanced 0.25–0.5 kg/month. If you're gaining faster you're likely storing more fat than muscle — muscle protein synthesis is biologically limited regardless of calorie intake.

faq.question: What is the difference between lean bulk and dirty bulk?
faq.answer: Lean bulk = controlled surplus (+150–350 kcal/day) → minimal fat gain, maintain definition, longer but more effective process. Dirty bulk = eating without limits → rapid weight gain but a large proportion is fat requiring a long cut afterwards. Lean bulk is almost always the better choice.

faq.question: How much protein is needed during bulk vs cut?
faq.answer: During bulk: 1.6–2.2 g/kg body weight/day — sufficient for muscle protein synthesis. During cut: 1.8–2.4 g/kg/day — slightly higher to counteract muscle catabolism during a calorie deficit. Protein is the most important macronutrient in both phases.

sources.text: Barakat C, et al. Body Recomposition: Can Trained Individuals Build Muscle and Lose Fat at the Same Time? Strength Cond J. 2020;42(5):7–21.

Morton RW, et al. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52(6):376–384.

schema.headline: Bulk and Cut — Calories for Muscle Building and Fat Loss
schema.description: How bulk and cut work, how many calories to eat in each phase and how to optimize your training cycle.

s1.p1: During a bulk you eat more calories than you burn. This creates an anabolic environment where the body can afford to build muscle tissue. Without a calorie surplus, muscle building is possible but considerably slower.
s1.p2: Optimal balance between muscle growth and minimal fat gain. Expected pace: approx. 0.2–0.4 kg per week (of which a large proportion is muscle in the first months).
s1.p3: Faster weight gain but a large proportion is fat. Works for hardgainers and beginners but for experienced athletes mostly results in fat storage that needs to be cut away again.

s2.p1: During a cut you eat below your TDEE to lose fat, with the goal of preserving maximum muscle mass. It requires discipline, adequate protein and strength training.
s2.p2: Recommended pace for most people. Gives 0.3–0.5 kg/week with good muscle mass preservation.
s2.p3Strong: 500–750 kcal/day below TDEE, shorter period (4–8 weeks).
s2.p3: More aggressive but time-limited — reduces the risk of adaptive thermogenesis. Requires high protein and strength training.

s3.p1: Instead of separate bulk/cut phases you can eat around maintenance intake and slowly build muscle and lose fat . It's slower but avoids the yo-yo effect.
s3.p2: Works best for: beginners, people with high body fat percentage, and those returning after a training break. Experienced athletes with low body fat get better results from separate phases.

s4.h2: How do you know when to switch phase?
items: End bulk when: Body fat percentage has become too high (approx. 15–18% for men, 25–30% for women). Strength plateaus despite calorie surplus.
End cut when: You've reached the desired body fat percentage. Weight loss plateaus despite calorie deficit. Performance drops markedly.
Calculate your TDEE with the calculator
Bulk: add 300 kcal → your bulk intake
Cut: subtract 400 kcal → your cut intake
Eat 1.8–2.2 g protein/kg in both phases
Strength train 3–4 times/week
Adjust the calorie goal every 2–3 weeks based on actual weight development

seo.title: Reverse Diet — What It Is and How to Increase Calories After Dieting (2026) | CalculEat
seo.description: A reverse diet means slowly increasing calorie intake after a cut to restore metabolism without storing fat. Learn when it's needed, how to do it and what the research says.

layout.title: Reverse Diet — What It Is and How to Increase Calories After Dieting
layout.intro: A reverse diet is a structured way to raise calorie intake after a cut — gradually, controlled, without storing unnecessary fat. It's not a fitness myth. It's a practical tool for those who have dieted aggressively and want to return to maintenance intake without rebounding in weight.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your maintenance needs (TDEE) as a starting point for reverse dieting

faq.question: What is a reverse diet?
faq.answer: A reverse diet is a phase after a cut where you gradually increase calorie intake by 50–100 kcal/week until you've reached your new maintenance needs (TDEE). The goal is to restore metabolism and leptin levels without rapidly storing fat.

faq.question: Does everyone need a reverse diet?
faq.answer: No. A reverse diet is most relevant for those who have dieted aggressively for a long time (>12 weeks with a large deficit), experience signs of adaptive thermogenesis (weight plateau despite deficit, fatigue, lower performance) or are planning a new bulk and want to maximize muscle growth potential.

faq.question: How fast do you increase calories during a reverse diet?
faq.answer: Typically 50–100 kcal/week until you reach your TDEE. This means 8–16 weeks to increase 500–800 kcal if you've dieted well below maintenance. Faster increases (200+ kcal/week) are possible but result in more fat gain and miss the point of a reverse diet.

faq.question: Can you gain weight during a reverse diet?
faq.answer: Yes — some weight gain is normal and expected, primarily from increased glycogen storage and water retention as carbohydrates increase. Actual fat gain should be minimal if done gradually. If you're rapidly gaining more than 0.5–1 kg per week you're likely increasing too fast.

faq.question: What is the difference between a reverse diet and a bulk?
faq.answer: A reverse diet takes you from a deficit to maintenance — the goal is to restore metabolism, not to build muscle. A bulk takes you from maintenance to a surplus for muscle building. A reverse diet may precede a bulk but is a distinct step.

sources.text: Trexler ET, Smith-Ryan AE, Norton LE. Metabolic adaptation to weight loss: implications for the athlete. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11(1):7.
Rosenbaum M, Leibel RL. Models of energy homeostasis in the context of obesity. Curr Opin Clin Nutr Metab Care. 2010;13(4):422–426.
Müller MJ, et al. Metabolic adaptation to caloric restriction and subsequent refeeding: the Minnesota Starvation Experiment revisited. Am J Clin Nutr. 2015;102(4):807–819.

schema.headline: Reverse Diet — What It Is and How to Increase Calories After Dieting
schema.description: A reverse diet means slowly increasing calorie intake after a cut to restore metabolism without storing fat.

s1.p1: A reverse diet is the process of gradually raising calorie intake after a period of calorie deficit (cut). Instead of going directly from e.g. 1,600 kcal/day to 2,300 kcal/day, you increase by 50–100 kcal per week until you reach your maintenance intake (TDEE).
s1.p2pre: The idea is based on a real physiological mechanism:
s1.p2: — the metabolic downregulation that occurs during prolonged periods of calorie deficit. The body lowers its NEAT (unplanned movement), thyroid hormones and leptin levels in response to energy shortage. This means your actual TDEE during the cut is lower than it was before.

s2.h2: When is a reverse diet relevant?
s2.p1: A reverse diet is most justified in these situations:
items: You have dieted aggressively for a long time (12+ weeks). The longer and more restrictive the diet was, the more pronounced the metabolic adaptation — and the more careful the transition should be.
You have clear signs of adaptive thermogenesis: fatigue, decreased performance, cold all the time, irregular menstrual cycle (women), plateau despite low calorie intake.

You are planning directly for a new bulk or muscle building phase. A controlled transition via reverse diet provides a better starting point for the bulk and reduces the risk of "rebound fat storage" with a sudden calorie increase.
Psychological need for structure. Many find that having a schedule for increase — rather than just "eating more" — reduces food anxiety after a long diet.
s2.items0strong: You have dieted aggressively for a long time (12+ weeks).
s2.items1strong: You have clear signs of adaptive thermogenesis:
s2.items2strong: You are planning directly for a new bulk or muscle building phase.

s3.h2: When a reverse diet is not needed
s3.p1: necessary in all situations and is sometimes unnecessarily complicated:
items: You have dieted at a moderate pace (−300–400 kcal/day) for 8–12 weeks — metabolic adaptation is probably minimal.
You have not lost more than 5–8% of body weight in total — no large hormonal disruption is expected.
You are planning a longer maintenance phase (3+ months) without a new weight goal immediately — the body recovers naturally.
s3.p2: In these cases you can go directly to your calculated TDEE without structuring a formal reverse diet.

s4.h2: Reverse diet, diet break and maintenance — what's the difference?

phases.def: Gradual increase of calorie intake (50–100 kcal/week) from cut intake up to TDEE. Lasts 4–12 weeks. Used after a long or aggressive cut.

Shorter period (1–2 weeks) at maintenance intake in the middle of an ongoing cut. The purpose is to temporarily restore leptin and metabolism — then the diet continues. A diet break is not a reverse diet.
Eating at your TDEE permanently, without a weight change goal. Can be reached directly or via reverse diet. Maintenance is the end goal of a reverse diet.

s5.h2: Step by step: how to do a reverse diet
items: Calculate your target TDEE. Use a TDEE calculator based on your current weight, height, age and activity level. This is your end goal — the calorie intake you gradually aim to reach.
Start with your current cut intake. If you end the cut at 1,700 kcal/day, start the reverse diet from there.
Increase by 50–100 kcal per week. Add the calories primarily to carbohydrates and fat — protein intake doesn't need to increase (maintain 1.6–2.2 g/kg).

Monitor your weight each week. Some increase is normal (water, glycogen). If weight rises more than 0.3 kg/week for more than 2 consecutive weeks — pause the increase for a week and see how the body responds.
Continue until you reach your TDEE. When you're eating at or close to TDEE and weight is stable — the reverse diet is complete. You are now in maintenance.
s5.items1strong: Start with your current cut intake.
s5.items4strong: Continue until you reach your TDEE.

items: Increasing too fast. +200–300 kcal/day immediately leads to rapid fat storage if the metabolism hasn't had time to recover. Take it slow.
Not counting protein. During a reverse diet it's tempting to add calories via candy or processed food. Keep protein high — it protects muscles and reduces fat storage during the calorie increase.
Confusing normal weight gain with fat storage. The first 1–2 kg gained are almost always water and glycogen, not fat. Don't panic.

Skipping reverse diet when it's actually needed. Going from 1,400 to 2,400 kcal directly after 16 weeks of aggressive cut increases the risk of "fat overshoot" — the body stores disproportionately much fat in response to the sudden energy surplus.
s6.items2strong: Confusing normal weight gain with fat storage.
s6.items3strong: Skipping reverse diet when it's actually needed.

seo.description: BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) is the calories your body burns at complete rest. Learn what BMR is, how it differs from TDEE and why you should never eat at your BMR.

layout.title: What is BMR? Basal Metabolic Rate Explained
layout.intro: BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) is the calories your body burns at complete rest — without movement, food or activity. It is the body's minimum energy requirement to keep the heart, lungs, brain and organs running. BMR is the foundation for calculating your actual calorie needs, but it is not the number you should eat at.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your actual calorie needs with the TDEE calculator

faq.question: What is the difference between BMR and TDEE?
faq.answer: BMR is your resting burn rate — the calories you need if you lay completely still all day. TDEE is your actual calorie needs including all movement and activity. TDEE = BMR × activity factor (PAL). For most people TDEE is 20–80% higher than BMR.

faq.question: Can you eat at your BMR?
faq.answer: No, it's not recommended. BMR is your resting burn rate — you burn more than this just by standing, walking and eating (TEF). Consistently eating at BMR means an aggressive calorie deficit, with risk of muscle mass loss, nutritional deficiency and metabolic downregulation.

faq.question: How is BMR calculated?
faq.answer: The most widely used formula is Mifflin-St Jeor (1990): Men: BMR = 10 × weight(kg) + 6.25 × height(cm) − 5 × age + 5. Women: BMR = 10 × weight(kg) + 6.25 × height(cm) − 5 × age − 161. This formula gives a margin of error of ±10% for most people.

faq.question: Does BMR decrease when you diet?
faq.answer: Yes — partly because BMR decreases due to lower body weight (you're carrying less mass to maintain), and partly because adaptive thermogenesis can lower BMR slightly beyond what's explained by weight loss. This is one of the reasons weight loss plateaus and why diet breaks are valuable.

faq.question: What raises BMR?
faq.answer: Muscle mass is the strongest BMR booster — muscles burn more energy at rest than fat. Strength training and adequate protein intake slow muscle mass loss during aging and dieting. Cold temperatures temporarily increase BMR (brown adipose tissue is activated).

sources.text: Mifflin MD, St Jeor ST, Hill LA, Scott BJ, Daugherty SA, Koh YO. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals. Am J Clin Nutr. 1990;51(2):241–247.
Harris JA, Benedict FG. A biometric study of human basal metabolism. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 1918;4(12):370–373.
Cunningham JJ. A reanalysis of the factors influencing basal metabolic rate in normal adults. Am J Clin Nutr. 1980;33(11):2372–2374.
Roza AM, Shizgal HM. The Harris Benedict equation reevaluated. Am J Clin Nutr. 1984;40(1):168–182.
Henry CJ. Basal metabolic rate studies in humans: measurement and development of new equations. Public Health Nutr. 2005;8(7A):1133–1152.
Trexler ET, Smith-Ryan AE, Norton LE. Metabolic adaptation to weight loss. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2014;11(1):7.

schema.headline: What is BMR? Basal Metabolic Rate Explained
schema.description: BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) is the calories your body burns at complete rest. Learn what BMR is and how it differs from TDEE.

s1.p1: The most important determinant of BMR is fat-free mass (FFM) — muscles, organs and skeleton. Fat-free mass is estimated to explain around 80% of the variation in BMR between individuals. This explains why well-trained people with high muscle mass have a higher BMR than people of the same total weight but more body fat.
s1.p2: In people with low physical activity, BMR typically constitutes about 60% of total energy expenditure, and even more in individuals with very low movement activity such as sedated and mechanically ventilated patients in intensive care units.
s1.p3: Other factors that affect BMR: age (BMR drops approx. 1–2% per decade from age 30 due to decreased muscle mass), gender (men on average have higher BMR per kg body weight thanks to higher proportion of muscle mass) and hormonal balance (primarily thyroid hormones).

s2.h2: How is BMR measured and calculated?
s2.p1: BMR is measured under strictly controlled laboratory conditions: after sleep, in a fasting state and in a thermoneutral environment. The gold standard is indirect calorimetry via Weir's equation (1949), which calculates energy expenditure from oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production.
s2.p2: In practical contexts, RMR (Resting Metabolic Rate) is more commonly used, measured at any time during the day, which can differ from BMR by up to 10%. Most online calculators — including CalculEat — technically calculate RMR, but use the term BMR in everyday use.
s2.p3: When direct measurement is unavailable, predictive equations are used. The most common are:
items: Mifflin-St Jeor (1990) — recommended for healthy adults, best accuracy in modern populations
Harris-Benedict (revised 1984) — older but still common
Cunningham (1991) — calculates RMR based on fat-free mass, better for well-trained individuals
s2.p4: All predictive formulas have a margin of error of ±10–15% at the individual level. Actual weight trend over 2–3 weeks is always a more reliable measure than formula-based estimates.

s3.h2: Why should you not eat at your BMR?
s3.p1: BMR is the absolute minimum — not a calorie goal. Eating exactly at BMR means giving the body precisely what it needs to survive at complete rest, but nothing for movement, digestion or normal daily activity.
s3.p2: The consequences of eating at BMR for an extended period include muscle mass loss, fatigue, hormonal disruptions and metabolic adaptation — the body lowers its own BMR to save energy. This makes weight loss increasingly difficult.
s3.p3pre: The right approach is to calculate your
s3.p3: (BMR × activity factor) and create a moderate deficit from there — typically 300–500 kcal/day for sustainable weight loss.

s4.h2: From BMR to calorie goal — step by step
items: Calculate your BMR with the Mifflin-St Jeor formula (age, gender, weight, height).
Multiply by your activity factor (PAL) — sedentary (×1.2) to extremely active (×1.9).
The result is your TDEE — your maintenance need.
Subtract 300–500 kcal/day for weight loss, or add 200–300 kcal/day for muscle building.

seo.title: BMR vs RMR — What Is the Difference? | CalculEat
seo.description: BMR and RMR both measure energy expenditure at rest but differ in measurement conditions. Learn the difference, which formulas calculate what and why it matters.

layout.title: BMR vs RMR — What Is the Difference?
layout.intro: BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) and RMR (Resting Metabolic Rate) are two terms often used interchangeably — but they are technically different things. The difference comes down to measurement conditions and is typically 5–10%. Here we explain what sets them apart, which formulas calculate what, and whether it matters for your calorie planning.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your BMR/RMR with the calculator

faq.question: Is BMR always lower than RMR?
faq.answer: Yes — BMR is measured under stricter conditions (fasting, thermoneutral environment, complete rest after sleep) and represents the body's absolute minimum. RMR is measured under more practical conditions and includes a little more activity. The difference is typically 5–10%, sometimes up to 20% in individuals with high NEAT.

faq.question: Which formula should you use?
faq.answer: Mifflin-St Jeor (1990) technically calculates RMR, not strict BMR, but is commonly called a BMR formula. It is the most validated formula for the general population. Harris-Benedict (revised) gives similar results. Cunningham (based on LBM) is best for athletes with known body fat percentage.

faq.question: Does it matter for calorie planning?
faq.answer: No, in practice. When you calculate TDEE (BMR/RMR × activity factor), the 5–10% difference is absorbed in the formulas' error margins and the activity factor's uncertainty. Use Mifflin-St Jeor as standard and then calibrate against your actual weight trend.

faq.question: Why is Mifflin-St Jeor called a BMR formula if it measures RMR?
faq.answer: The terminology in the literature is inconsistent. Mifflin et al. (1990) calibrated against RMR measurements but labelled it as RMR. Popularization in nutrition and fitness contexts then tagged the results as 'BMR'. For practical calorie planning it's the same thing.

faq.question: Can you measure BMR/RMR at home?
faq.answer: Indirectly — via calorimetry devices (e.g. BodyGem, MedGem) that measure oxygen consumption. These are reasonably accurate but cost thousands of dollars. Home formulas (Mifflin-St Jeor etc.) give typically ±10% margin of error, which is acceptable for calorie planning.

sources.text: Mifflin MD, et al. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure. Am J Clin Nutr. 1990;51(2):241–247.
Weir JB. New methods for calculating metabolic rate with special reference to protein metabolism. J Physiol. 1949;109(1–2):1–9.
Frankenfield D, Roth-Yousey L, Compher C. Comparison of predictive equations for resting metabolic rate in healthy nonobese and obese adults. J Am Diet Assoc. 2005;105(5):775–789.

schema.headline: BMR vs RMR — What Is the Difference?
schema.description: BMR and RMR both measure energy expenditure at rest but differ in measurement conditions. Learn the difference and which formulas calculate what.

s1.p1: BMR is measured under extremely controlled conditions: after at least 8 hours of sleep, 12 hours of fasting and in a thermoneutral environment (~22°C). Under these conditions the body is literally at its lowest possible energy level.
s1.p2: RMR is measured in realistic rest — you are relaxed and still, but not necessarily fasting or just woken up. The body still maintains some muscle tension, may be processing a meal and adjusting to room temperature. This gives marginally higher energy expenditure — typically 5–10% above BMR.

s2.h2: Does the difference matter in practice?
s2.p1: Rarely. All predictive formulas have a margin of error of ±10–15% at the individual level — that's already larger than the difference between BMR and RMR. The distinction is relevant in clinical research and with indirect calorimetry, but for everyday calorie planning it's unimportant which concept a formula technically calculates.
s2.p2: What actually matters: choose a formula, multiply by the correct PAL factor to get your TDEE, and monitor your weight trend for 2–3 weeks. Actual weight change is always more reliable than formula-based estimates.

seo.title: BMR vs TDEE — What Is the Difference and Which Should You Use? | CalculEat
seo.description: BMR is your resting burn rate. TDEE is what you actually burn per day. Learn the difference and why you should always plan calories based on TDEE — not BMR.

layout.title: BMR vs TDEE — What Is the Difference and Which Should You Use?
layout.intro: BMR is your resting burn rate — the calories your body needs at complete rest. TDEE is what you actually burn over an entire day, including movement, exercise and digestion. This is an important distinction: you should always plan calories based on TDEE, never BMR.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your TDEE directly — free calculator

faq.question: Can you eat at your BMR?
faq.answer: No — BMR is your absolute resting burn rate. You burn more energy just by standing, walking and eating (TEF ≈ 10% of calorie intake). Eating at BMR means an aggressive calorie deficit with risk of muscle loss and metabolic downregulation.

faq.question: How large is the difference between BMR and TDEE?
faq.answer: Typically 20–80% depending on activity level. A sedentary person (PAL 1.2) has a TDEE that is 20% above BMR. An extremely active person (PAL 1.9) has a TDEE that is 90% above BMR. The average for a normally active adult is about 40–50% above BMR.

faq.question: Do you calculate a calorie deficit against BMR or TDEE?
faq.answer: Always against TDEE. A calorie deficit is by definition eating below your total daily energy needs (TDEE). If you calculate a deficit against BMR you're actually eating enormously below your real needs.

faq.question: Why is BMR used if TDEE is the relevant measure?
faq.answer: BMR is the starting point in the calculation — a measurable baseline value that is then multiplied by an activity factor to give TDEE. BMR alone is not useful for calorie planning, but it is the scientific foundation for all TDEE calculations.

faq.question: Does the BMR/TDEE relationship change with age?
faq.answer: Yes. BMR drops about 1–2% per decade after age 20 (muscle mass loss). Activity level also tends to decrease. The result is that TDEE drops more than BMR in relative terms — but the BMR/TDEE ratio remains roughly the same if the activity pattern is unchanged.

sources.text: Mifflin MD, et al. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure. Am J Clin Nutr. 1990;51(2):241–247.
Ainsworth BE, et al. 2011 Compendium of Physical Activities. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2011;43(8):1575–1581.
Pontzer H, et al. Daily energy expenditure through the human life course. Science. 2021;373(6556):808–812.

schema.headline: BMR vs TDEE — What Is the Difference and Which Should You Use?
schema.description: BMR is your resting burn rate. TDEE is what you actually burn per day. Learn the difference and why you should always plan calories based on TDEE.

s1.p1: BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) is the calories your body burns at complete rest — without movement, digestion or external activity. It is the energy that goes to keeping the heart, lungs, brain and organs running.
s1.p2: BMR is calculated with formulas like Mifflin-St Jeor or Harris-Benedict, based on gender, age, weight and height. It is the starting point for all calorie calculations — but it is not the number you should eat at.

s2.p1: TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is the calories you actually burn during a day — including all movement and activity. TDEE is calculated as:
s2.p2: PAL (Physical Activity Level) ranges from 1.3 for sedentary to 2.1 or more for very active. TDEE includes planned exercise (EAT), spontaneous movement (NEAT) and the energy cost of digestion (TEF).

s4.h2: Why you should always use TDEE
s4.p1: Planning calories based on BMR creates an uncontrolled deficit. Example: a person with BMR 1,700 kcal and TDEE 2,400 kcal who eats 1,700 kcal thinks they are at maintenance — but are actually in a 700 kcal deficit.
s4.p2: This leads to rapid weight loss initially, but with significant muscle mass loss and metabolic adaptation. The body lowers BMR to save energy, making it harder to sustain weight loss.
s4.p3: Right approach: calculate your TDEE and create a controlled deficit of — sufficient for sustainable weight loss without sacrificing muscle mass.

seo.title: BMI vs Body Fat — Which Measurement Is Most Accurate? | CalculEat
seo.description: BMI measures weight in relation to height. Body fat measures actual fat percentage. Learn when BMI misses the mark and when you need a more precise measure to set the right calorie goal.

layout.title: BMI vs Body Fat — Which Measurement Is Most Accurate?
layout.intro: BMI (Body Mass Index) is easy to calculate but only measures weight in relation to height — not how weight is distributed. Body fat measures the actual proportion of fat in the body and gives a more complete picture. Both have their uses, but they answer different questions.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your calorie needs with the TDEE calculator

faq.question: Which measure is better — BMI or body fat?
faq.answer: Body fat is more informative for most purposes. BMI can misjudge health in muscular individuals (classified as overweight), older people (low muscle mass gives normal BMI despite high body fat) and shorter people. Body fat directly addresses what actually matters for health risk.

faq.question: Can you have a normal BMI but high body fat?
faq.answer: Yes — this is called 'normal-weight obesity' or 'skinny fat'. It's relatively common in people with little muscle mass. A person at 170 cm and 65 kg has BMI 22.5 (normal weight) but can have 30% body fat if they have little muscle mass.

faq.question: Can you have a high BMI but low body fat?
faq.answer: Yes — muscular individuals are often classified as 'overweight' on the BMI scale despite low body fat and excellent health. A well-trained person at 175 cm and 85 kg (BMI 27.8) can have 12% body fat and be in excellent shape.

faq.question: Which measure should you use to set a calorie goal?
faq.answer: Neither BMI nor body fat alone. TDEE (your actual calorie needs) is the starting point for calorie planning. Body fat is valuable information for understanding where you are and where you want to go — but the calorie goal is set against TDEE, not against a body fat percentage.

sources.text: Romero-Corral A, et al. Accuracy of body mass index in diagnosing obesity in the adult general population. Int J Obes (Lond). 2008;32(6):959–966.
Gallagher D, et al. Healthy percentage body fat ranges. Am J Clin Nutr. 2000;72(3):694–701.
Flegal KM, et al. Comparisons of percentage body fat, body mass index, waist circumference, and waist-stature ratio in adults. Am J Clin Nutr. 2009;89(2):500–508.

schema.headline: BMI vs Body Fat — Which Measurement Is Most Accurate?
schema.description: BMI measures weight in relation to height. Body fat measures actual fat percentage. Learn when BMI misses the mark.

s1.p1: BMI is calculated as weight (kg) divided by height² (m²). The result is placed in one of four categories: underweight (below 18.5), normal weight (18.5–24.9), overweight (25–29.9) or obese (30+).
s1.p2: The advantage of BMI is its simplicity — you only need weight and height. The disadvantage is that it doesn't distinguish between muscle mass and fat tissue. A well-trained person with high muscle mass can end up in the "overweight" category according to BMI despite low body fat percentage.

s2.p1: Body fat is the proportion of your body weight that consists of fat tissue. It is measured with methods such as the US Navy method (based on body measurements), skinfold measurement, bioimpedance or DEXA (X-ray). DEXA is the gold standard but requires specialist equipment.
s2.p2: Body fat gives a more precise picture of body composition — how much is muscle, fat, bone and fluid. This is particularly important for people with high muscle mass (athletes, powerlifters) where BMI systematically overestimates health risk.

s4.h2: When BMI is sufficient — and when it misses
s4.p1: BMI works as a rough screening tool at the population level and for most normal-weight people without extremely high or low muscle mass. It's quick, free and requires no equipment.
items: Muscular individuals (trained, athletes, powerlifters)
Older people with low muscle mass but normal weight ("sarcopenic obesity")
Pregnant women
Children and adolescents (require age-specific reference values)
Individuals with very low muscle mass and high body fat percentage ("skinny fat")

s5.p1: Regardless of which measure you look at — BMI or body fat — your calorie goal is the practical tool for getting there. The calorie goal is based on your TDEE, not on BMI or body fat percentage per se. Calculate your TDEE to get a figure you can actually act on.

seo.title: What is FFMI? Fat-Free Mass Index Explained | CalculEat
seo.description: FFMI (Fat-Free Mass Index) measures muscle mass relative to height — independent of body fat percentage. Learn what FFMI is, how it's calculated and what natural limits mean.

layout.title: What is FFMI? Fat-Free Mass Index Explained
layout.intro: FFMI (Fat-Free Mass Index) measures your fat-free muscle mass relative to your height. Unlike BMI, FFMI is not affected by your body fat percentage — it is a pure measure of muscle development. FFMI is used to assess training level and, in research, to distinguish natural athletes from those who use performance-enhancing drugs.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your calorie needs for muscle building

faq.question: What is a normal FFMI?
faq.answer: For untrained men: 18–20. For untrained women: 14–16. With 3–5 years of consistent strength training, natural lifters can reach 21–23 (men) and 17–19 (women). Normalized FFMI above 25 (men) is statistically rare naturally.

faq.question: Why can't FFMI be calculated without body fat percentage?
faq.answer: FFMI = (weight × (1 − body fat/100)) ÷ height². Without body fat you don't know what proportion of your weight is fat-free mass (muscle, organs, bone). That's why the FFMI calculator requires a body fat estimate, preferably measured with the US Navy method.

faq.question: Is FFMI 25 a hard limit for natural athletes?
faq.answer: No — it's a statistical observation, not a biological limit. Kouri et al. (1995) found that natural athletes rarely exceeded normalized FFMI 25. Individuals with exceptional genetics and skeletal structure can reach 25–26 naturally. But it's rare enough to be a statistically significant outlier.

faq.question: How does FFMI differ from BMI?
faq.answer: BMI = weight ÷ height². It is affected by body fat percentage and doesn't distinguish between muscle and fat. FFMI = fat-free mass ÷ height². It is a pure muscle mass measure. A well-trained person with high BMI (classified as overweight) can have a low FFMI if they have little muscle, and vice versa.

faq.question: Can you improve FFMI without gaining weight?
faq.answer: Yes — via body recomposition (building muscle and burning fat simultaneously). FFMI increases when fat-free mass increases relative to weight. It's slower than a dedicated bulk but possible, especially for beginners and those returning to training after a break.

sources.text: Kouri EM, Pope HG Jr, Katz DL, Oliva P. Fat-free mass index in users and nonusers of anabolic-androgenic steroids. Clin J Sport Med. 1995;5(4):223–228.
Schutz Y, Kyle UU, Pichard C. Fat-free mass index and fat mass index percentiles in Caucasians aged 18-98 y. Int J Obes Relat Metab Disord. 2002;26(7):953–960.

schema.headline: What is FFMI? Fat-Free Mass Index Explained
schema.description: FFMI (Fat-Free Mass Index) measures muscle mass relative to height. Learn what FFMI is and what natural limits mean.

s1.h2: How do you improve your FFMI?
s1.p1: FFMI increases when you build muscle mass — it's that simple. In practice it requires a combination of consistent strength training, adequate protein intake (1.6–2.2 g/kg body weight) and a slight calorie surplus (bulk).
s1.p2: Important: reducing body fat percentage without building muscle does not improve FFMI — it remains unchanged. FFMI measures only fat-free mass, not how your body looks in the mirror.
s1.p3: Calculate your TDEE to set the right calorie goal — either a small surplus for muscle building, or maintenance intake with a focus on strength training.

seo.title: What is PAL and MET? Activity Level and Energy Expenditure Explained | CalculEat
seo.description: PAL (Physical Activity Level) and MET (Metabolic Equivalent of Task) are two ways to measure activity level. Learn how they're used to calculate TDEE and calorie needs.

layout.title: What is PAL and MET? Activity Level and Energy Expenditure Explained
layout.intro: PAL (Physical Activity Level) is the activity factor multiplied by BMR to give your TDEE — your actual calorie needs. MET (Metabolic Equivalent of Task) measures how intense a specific activity is relative to rest. Both are used to calculate energy expenditure, but in different ways.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your TDEE with the right activity level

faq.question: What is the difference between PAL and MET?
faq.answer: PAL (Physical Activity Level) is a daily average factor multiplied by BMR to give TDEE. PAL 1.2 = sedentary, PAL 1.9 = extremely active. MET (Metabolic Equivalent of Task) measures energy expenditure for a single activity relative to rest (1 MET = resting energy). PAL is a daily average; MET is activity-specific.

faq.question: How do you choose the right PAL factor?
faq.answer: PAL 1.2 (Sedentary): office work, minimal movement. PAL 1.375 (Lightly active): light exercise 1–3 days/week. PAL 1.55 (Moderately active): exercise 3–5 days/week. PAL 1.725 (Very active): hard training 6–7 days/week. PAL 1.9 (Extremely active): physical work + daily intense training. Choose honestly based on your total weekly activity.

faq.question: Can you calculate TDEE with MET values instead of PAL?
faq.answer: Yes — TDEE = BMR × PAL, or alternatively: sum energy expenditure per activity via MET values (Energy kcal = MET × weight(kg) × time(h)) and add BMR × 24 for resting burn. The MET method is more accurate for specific exercise periods but more complex to apply daily.

faq.question: Why do PAL factors differ between individuals?
faq.answer: NEAT (Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis) — unplanned movement like fidgeting, standing, walking — varies enormously (200–800 kcal/day) and significantly affects PAL. Two people with identical exercise routines but different NEAT can have PAL factors differing by 0.2–0.3 units.

sources.text: FAO/WHO/UNU. Human energy requirements. Report of a Joint Expert Consultation. Rome, 2004.
Ainsworth BE, et al. 2011 Compendium of Physical Activities: a second update of codes and MET values. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2011;43(8):1575–1581.
Levine JA. Non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT). Best Pract Res Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2002;16(4):679–702.

schema.headline: What is PAL and MET? Activity Level and Energy Expenditure Explained
schema.description: PAL and MET are two ways to measure activity level. Learn how they're used to calculate TDEE and calorie needs.

s1.h2: Choose the right PAL for your calorie goal
s1.p1: The most common mistake in TDEE calculation is overestimating your activity level. If you train 3 days per week but sit still the rest of the day, you are probably "lightly active" (PAL 1.375) — not "moderately active" (PAL 1.55).
s1.p2: A practical method: start with a conservative PAL value and increase if your weight drops faster than planned. It's easier to adjust up than to handle an excessively large calorie deficit.
s1.p3: Try our TDEE calculator to calculate your calorie needs with different activity levels and see how large the difference actually is.

seo.title: LBM vs FFM — The Difference Between Lean Body Mass and Fat Free Mass | CalculEat
seo.description: LBM and FFM both describe the body's non-fat mass but are not identical. Learn what sets them apart and which measure to use in your calculations.

layout.title: LBM vs FFM — What Is the Difference?
layout.intro: LBM (Lean Body Mass) and FFM (Fat Free Mass) are often used synonymously, but they don't measure exactly the same thing. Both describe the body's non-fat mass — but the definition of 'fat' differs in a way that actually matters when choosing a formula or interpreting a measurement result.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your body composition with our calculator

faq.question: What is the difference between LBM and FFM?
faq.answer: FFM (Fat Free Mass) = all tissue minus all fat (including essential fat in cell membranes, nerve tissue etc.). LBM (Lean Body Mass) = FFM + essential fat (about 3% for men, 12% for women). In practice, LBM > FFM by about 3–12% depending on gender. For most calorie planning purposes the difference is not clinically relevant.

faq.question: Which measure is used in BMR formulas?
faq.answer: The Cunningham formula (the only LBM-based BMR formula in common use) technically uses LBM: BMR = 500 + 22 × LBM(kg). In practice, LBM and FFM are used synonymously in most formula contexts.

faq.question: Do you need to know your LBM to calculate calorie needs?
faq.answer: No — not for Mifflin-St Jeor or Harris-Benedict, which only use total weight, height, age and gender. LBM is needed for the Cunningham formula and for more advanced protein planning (g/kg LBM instead of g/kg total weight).

faq.question: How do you measure LBM/FFM?
faq.answer: DEXA scanning is the gold standard. Hydrostatic weighing, air displacement plethysmography (BOD POD) and MRI provide high precision. The US Navy method (as our calculator uses) gives an estimate with ±3–4% margin of error — sufficient for calorie planning.

sources.text: Heymsfield SB, et al. Human body composition. Human Kinetics, 2005.
Cunningham JJ. A reanalysis of the factors influencing basal metabolic rate in normal adults. Am J Clin Nutr. 1980;33(11):2372–2374.
Wang ZM, et al. The five-level model: a new approach to organizing body-composition research. Am J Clin Nutr. 1992;56(1):19–28.

schema.headline: LBM vs FFM — What Is the Difference?
schema.description: LBM and FFM both describe the body's non-fat mass but are not identical. Learn what sets them apart.

s1.h2: What is LBM — Lean Body Mass?
s1.p1: LBM is everything in the body except body fat. That sounds like a simple definition, but the key lies in the word : LBM includes the fat the body cannot do without — essential fat.
items: Organs (heart, liver, kidneys)
The brain and nervous system
Cell membranes throughout the body
s1.p3: This fat is structurally and functionally necessary — it cannot be reduced without disrupting the body's basic processes. It is therefore counted as part of the "lean" mass in the LBM definition.

s2.h2: What is FFM — Fat Free Mass?
s2.p1: FFM is a stricter definition: completely fat-free tissue. No fat is included — not even essential fat. FFM consists of:
items: Muscles
Organs (without adipose tissue)
Body fluid and water
Skeleton and minerals
s2.p2: FFM is thus a purer biochemical definition — the mass you would have left if all fat were eliminated, including what the body actually needs.

s3.boxLBM: LBM — includes essential fat (organs, brain, cell membranes)
s3.boxFFM: FFM — completely fat-free, no form of fat included
s3.p1: For a person at 80 kg with 15% body fat, LBM is approx. 2–3 kg higher than FFM. In most practical contexts — calculating calorie needs, protein intake or training load — that difference is negligible. But it's important to know which measure a given formula expects.

s4.p1: Most measurement methods — DEXA, bioimpedance and calipers — return FFM, not LBM. FFM is the standard measure in research and clinical practice.
s4.p2: Practical consequence: if a formula asks for "fat-free mass", it is FFM you should enter — that is, the value you get directly from your measurement. The Cunningham equation for RMR is a typical example: it is built on FFM and gives more accurate results for well-trained individuals than Mifflin-St Jeor, which only uses total weight.
s4.p3: If you don't know which measure your measurement method gives — assume FFM. It is the most common output and matches the formulas you are likely to use.

seo.title: How to Measure Body Fat? Methods and Accuracy Explained | CalculEat
seo.description: Learn the most common methods for measuring body fat — DEXA, bioimpedance, calipers and the Navy method — and what a good body fat percentage looks like.

layout.title: How to Measure Body Fat?
layout.intro: Body weight says little about the body — body fat percentage says more. Two people can weigh exactly the same but have completely different body compositions. Here we go through the most common methods for measuring body fat, how accurate they are and what the numbers actually mean.
layout.moneyPageLabel: Calculate your body fat percentage with the Navy method

faq.question: Which method for measuring body fat is most accurate?
faq.answer: DEXA scanning (Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry) is the gold standard with ±1–2% margin of error. It measures bone, fat and soft tissue separately using X-rays. Downsides: costs $50–200, requires a clinic. For home use, the US Navy method (±3–4%) is a good alternative.

faq.question: Are bioimpedance scales reliable?
faq.answer: Consumer scales with bioimpedance have typically ±5–8% margin of error and are strongly affected by hydration status — eating a little salt or drinking a lot of water makes the results vary markedly. They're useful for tracking trends if you always measure under the same conditions (morning, fasting, after using the bathroom). Absolute values are unreliable.

faq.question: What is a good body fat percentage?
faq.answer: Benchmarks: Men — athletic 6–13%, fit 14–17%, average 18–24%, overweight 25–29%, obese ≥30%. Women — athletic 14–20%, fit 21–24%, average 25–31%, overweight 32–39%, obese ≥40%. These are population-based benchmarks, not medical thresholds.

faq.question: How often should you measure body fat?
faq.answer: Every 4–8 weeks is sufficient. Daily measurements give too much noise due to fluid variations. The most important thing is to measure consistently: same method, same time of day (morning, fasting), same measurement points.

faq.question: Can you see abs without having a low body fat percentage?
faq.answer: No — abs require a low enough body fat percentage (typically below 14–16% for men, 18–22% for women) and sufficient muscle mass. Genetics, fat distribution and lighting affect how visible they are. It's not the body fat percentage alone that determines it, but the combination of body fat + muscle mass.

faq.question: Why do body fat measurements vary so much?
faq.answer: Different methods measure different things and have different error margins. Additionally, body fat varies with time of day, hydration status, food intake and menstrual cycle (for women). Focus on trends over time with one consistent method, not absolute values from different methods.

schema.headline: How to Measure Body Fat?
schema.description: Learn the most common methods for measuring body fat — DEXA, bioimpedance, calipers and the Navy method — and what the numbers actually mean.

s1.p1: Body weight is a blunt measure. A person who loses fat and builds muscle can see their weight stand still — or even increase — despite the body changing in the right direction. Body fat percentage gives a better picture of what's actually happening.
s1.p2: Body fat is measured as the proportion of fat tissue out of total weight. The rest is fat-free mass (FFM): muscles, skeleton, organs and water. It is the distribution between these that determines health, performance and appearance — not total weight itself.

s2.p1: The most common categorisations for body fat percentage (American Council on Exercise):
s2.note: Essential fat is biologically necessary — it exists in organs, brain and cell membranes and must never be undercut.

s3.h2: Measurement methods — from gold standard to home solution
s3.p1: DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) is the most accurate method available outside a laboratory. A low-dose X-ray distinguishes fat, muscle and bone mass throughout the body and provides a detailed map — including how fat is distributed regionally (abdomen, legs, arms).
s3.p1b: Extremely accurate, also measures bone mineral density, reproducible.
s3.p1c: Costs $50–150, requires a clinic, weak radiation exposure. Best suited for baseline measurement and follow-up every 6–12 months.
s3.p2: Historically considered the gold standard. The body is weighed underwater — the difference from air weight gives body density which is converted to body fat via the Siri equation (1961). Now almost completely replaced by DEXA for practical use.
s3.p3: A weak electrical current is passed through the body. Fat conducts electricity less well than muscle and water, and the resistance is used to estimate body fat. Found in everything from home scales to clinical InBody machines.
s3.p4: Accuracy varies greatly with hydration, last meal, caffeine and time of day. An InBody at a clinic is considerably more reliable than a home scale.
s3.p4b: Always measure in the morning, fasting and after visiting the bathroom — the same time each time. This minimises variability and makes the trend meaningful.
s3.p5: Several formulas calculate body fat solely from body measurements with a tape measure — no special instruments needed. The most common is the US Navy method (Hodgdon & Beckett, 1984), which measures waist circumference, neck circumference and (for women) hip circumference and calculates body fat via a logarithmic formula. Other tape-measure-based methods use different combinations of measurement points and give somewhat varying results.
s3.p6: The advantage is that it's completely free and can be done at home. The accuracy is sufficient to follow the trend, which is the most important thing for most people.
s3.p7: Calipers measure skinfold thickness at specific points — usually 3, 4 or 7 measurement points depending on the protocol (e.g. Jackson-Pollock). The results are entered into a formula that estimates total body fat percentage. Accuracy depends greatly on the measurer's technique and consistency — an experienced trainer or nutritionist gives more reliable results than self-measurement.
s3.p8: With profile data — age, gender, BMI and activity level — body fat can be estimated via population-based formulas (e.g. Deurenberg). This requires no measurement instruments at all but gives the lowest individual precision and is best used as a rough orientation.
s3.p9: A complementary way to calibrate your estimate is to compare with reference images — photographs of real bodies with known measured body fat percentage. This gives a visual anchor that numbers alone cannot provide.

s4.p1: It depends on what you want to achieve and what resources you have:
items: Best precision: DEXA — do a baseline measurement and follow-up every 3–6 months.
Regular home follow-up: Tape measure method, caliper measurement or a consistent bioimpedance scale under identical conditions each time.
Clinical follow-up: InBody (BIA) at a gym or clinic — more reliable than home scales.
Quick orientation without instruments: Profile-based estimation or comparison with reference images gives a rough but quick picture.
s4.p2: With a personal account in CalculEat you get access to all methods — several tape measure formulas, caliper protocols and profile-based estimation — as well as reference images for visual calibration. This makes it easy to choose the right method for your situation and follow the trend over time in one place.
s4.p3: The absolute value is always less important than the trend. Choose one method, stick to it and measure under identical conditions each time.
